extraction.name: POPE
extraction.description: A polling-based object probing evaluation method for assessing object hallucination in large vision-language models. It converts hallucination evaluation into a binary classification task using yes/no questions about probing objects.
extraction.creator: Yifan Li, Yifan Du, Kun Zhou, Jinpeng Wang, Wayne Xin Zhao, and Ji-Rong Wen
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The evaluation dataset was created by randomly sampling 2,000 images from the MSCOCO validation set and constructing POPE triples for each image consisting of the image, multiple yes/no object-probing questions, and answers. Existing object annotations, human-labeled captions, and optionally automatic segmentation outputs were used to obtain objects; negative questions were generated via random, popular, or adversarial sampling, with a 1:1 balance between ground-truth and nonexistent objects.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw/source data consisted of MSCOCO validation-set images together with annotations of contained objects and human-labeled captions; object candidates could also come from automatic segmentation results such as SEEM.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Ground-truth object annotations in MSCOCO are used as reference labels for evaluating hallucination; the proposed POPE evaluation converts hallucination assessment into a binary yes/no probing task about whether an object is present in the image.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Annotation/evaluation analysis is based on CHAIR metrics, including CHAIR_I at the object-instance level and CHAIR_S at the sentence level.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The paper identifies bias toward hallucinating objects that are frequent or frequently co-occurring in the visual instruction data, driven by unbalanced object distributions in datasets such as MSCOCO and synthetic instruction data.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The study focuses only on coarse-grained object hallucinations and leaves finer-grained errors such as object number, attributes, and positions for future work. It also notes that the existing CHAIR evaluation can be unstable across instructions and may introduce misclassification errors due to human-crafted parsing rules.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: Object hallucination may hinder safe real-world deployment of LVLMs and can cause harmful consequences, including safety risks in applications such as autonomous driving.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is used for evaluation of object hallucination in LVLMs, specifically by generating captions or answering yes/no probing questions on MSCOCO images using CHAIR and the proposed POPE method.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Images in MSCOCO were prompted with two caption-generation instructions, and the generated captions were then evaluated using the CHAIR metric to identify hallucinated objects.
